title: Remesh after you texture, not before. Fixed months of bad assets for me.
author: nosark
selftext:
I've been generating assets for my game (apes hauling cargo, working title *Remote Delivery*) and I ran the same three steps for months without questioning them: generate → remesh → texture.

I generated a properly beat-up parcel — dented corners, worn tape across the top flaps. Looked great. Remeshed it, textured it, dropped it in the scene, admired it from the front. Then rotated it.

Nothing on the bottom. No seam, no tape, no crease. Flat cardboard-colored nothing.

The reason, as far as I can tell: when you remesh first, you're handing the texturing step a clean simplified shape with no memory of the original generation's seams and creases. So it invents a surface, and it doesn't really understand that the tape on the sides connects to the tape on the bottom.

**Generate → texture → remesh** instead. Texture the model *before* you reduce it. The detail is already committed in the high detail model, so the remesh has to carry it through rather than reimagine it.

The catch: remeshing a textured model is messier. I got a handful of stray floating faces and I clean those up in Blender.

The broader thing this made me think about: a lot of what gets called slop is just careless editing. Not all of it — the training data argument is separate and I'm not pretending this addresses it. But there's a category of "something's off about this asset" that's purely craft, and it's craft the tools make very cheap to skip. My box's blank underside wasn't a hidden flaw, it was a flaw on a timer, because physics means packages land upside down in the mud eventually.

Curious if others have found similar ordering gotchas. Anything else in the pipeline where their sequence is backwards?

*Disclosure: I'm a Meshy Contributor, so they give me some free tokens for the articles I write about them.*

comments.author: deific_
comments.body:
Ive been using meshy for my models and wondered about this.  It’s not clear what the workflow is supposed to be.  I’m also trying to tackle the issue with hard surfaces getting crinkles and long triangles with you remesh down the poly count. I’ve tried blender decimate and it was not all that helpful.

It’s also taking me so many iterations to keep at consistent across items as well as interlocking pieces with a defined count that need to match.  It seems to have no idea how to count.

replies.author: nosark
replies.body: Have you joined their discord?  Lots of helpful people there.

replies.author: deific_
replies.body: I have not. Maybe I will.

comments.author: Dekker3D
comments.body: You can probably automate the Blender step. A simple Python script can select the geometry with the largest number of connected vertices, and just delete every other isolated bit that's less than 10% of that vertex count. If there's any part that's >10% but not the biggest geometry, then it should throw out a warning. Your AI agent can probably write this script for you and run it through Blender (or do it on its own, I guess).

replies.author: nosark
replies.body: I also think meshy could add a "remove floating vertices" step or name AI repair work on textured models.
